sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Medical imaging is an essential component of oncology, providing critical information 
for cancer diagnosis, staging, treatment planning, and therapy monitoring. Various 
imaging modalities, including computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging 
(MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), ultrasound (US), and histopathology, are 
routinely used in clinical practice to assess tumor characteristics and guide therapeu -
tic decisions [1–3]. The accuracy and reliability of imaging interpretation are crucial for 
effective patient management; yet conventional image analysis relies heavily on human 
expertise, which can be subject to inter-observer variability and time constraints [4].
Machine learning (ML) has gained significant attention in medical imaging due to 
its ability to automate and enhance image analysis [ 5, 6]. ML methods, particularly 
deep learning (DL) approaches such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have 
Discover Computing
Abstract
Machine learning (ML) is transforming cancer imaging by enhancing diagnosis, 
automating image analysis, and improving treatment planning. This review explores 
key ML applications, including tumor detection, radiomics, multi-modal imaging, 
and therapy monitoring. We discuss fundamental ML techniques, deep learning 
architectures, and data preprocessing strategies essential for medical imaging. 
ML-driven approaches have improved tumor segmentation, feature extraction, and 
computer-aided diagnosis across various cancer types. In cancer therapy, artificial 
intelligence (AI) aids radiotherapy planning, treatment response prediction, and 
real-time image-guided interventions. However, challenges such as data scarcity, 
model bias, and regulatory hurdles limit clinical adoption. Emerging solutions 
include explainable AI, federated learning for data privacy, and quantum computing 
for advanced imaging. Addressing these challenges through interdisciplinary 
collaboration will accelerate AI integration into clinical practice, enhancing cancer 
diagnosis and treatment.
Keywords Machine learning, Cancer imaging, Deep learning, Radiomics, Artificial 
intelligence, Diagnosis, Therapy planning, Medical imaging

demonstrated promising results in tasks such as tumor detection, segmentation, clas -
sification, and outcome prediction [7, 8]. These techniques have the potential to improve 
diagnostic accuracy, reduce workload for radiologists and radiation oncologist, and facil-
itate personalized treatment planning. Moreover, ML-driven radiomics [ 9, 10], which 
involves extracting quantitative features from medical images, has opened new possibili-
ties for non-invasive tumor characterization and treatment response assessment.
In cancer therapy, ML applications extend beyond diagnosis to treatment planning and 
monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted radiotherapy planning [ 11], predictive 
modeling of treatment responses [12], and real-time image-guided interventions [13] are 
actively being explored to enhance precision and adaptability in oncology. While ML-
based models show potential, their clinical translation is challenged by factors such as 
data availability, model interpretability, and regulatory approval [ 14]. Addressing these 
challenges is essential for integrating ML into routine clinical workflows and ensuring its 
reliability in medical decision-making.
This topical review provides an overview of ML applications in cancer imaging, dis -
cussing key methodologies, current advancements, and challenges. The role of ML in 
tumor detection, segmentation, radiomics, and therapy planning is examined, along 
with emerging trends such as explainable AI (XAI) [ 15], federated learning [16], and the 
integration of quantum computing [ 17]. By summarizing the current state of research 
and identifying future directions, this review aims to contribute to the ongoing develop -
ment of ML-driven cancer imaging solutions.
While prior reviews have offered valuable overviews of ML in cancer diagnostics and 
treatment [18–20], our review distinguishes itself by focusing on the integration of ML 
architectures into closed-loop, adaptive imaging-treatment workflows. We also highlight 
translational bottlenecks, such as data privacy, explainability, and workflow feedback 
cycles, as key enablers for clinical adoption, areas often not emphasized in more algo -
rithm-centric or diagnostic-focused reviews.
This review makes several scientific contributions that extend beyond architectural 
surveys and aim to bridge technical development with clinical translation in cancer 
imaging and therapy. First, it proposes a workflow-oriented synthesis that maps ML 
models to distinct stages of the oncology pipeline, from image acquisition and prepro -
cessing to radiogenomic modeling and therapy monitoring. This structure provides 
conceptual clarity and emphasizes clinical integration. Second, the review identifies key 
translational challenges, such as interpretability, generalizability, and feedback-driven 
adaptation, and integrates them into the evaluation of current ML methods. Third, it 
contextualizes emerging fields such as XAI, federated learning, and quantum machine 
learning within the oncology domain, offering insights into how these technologies may 
enhance robustness, privacy, and computational efficiency. Finally, the review high -
lights the critical need for closed-loop, adaptive AI systems that respond dynamically to 
imaging feedback, offering a vision for future intelligent platforms that not only predict 
outcomes but iteratively refine their guidance based on treatment response. These con -
tributions collectively aim to support interdisciplinary advancement by aligning techni -
cal innovation with clinical priorities and regulatory considerations.
Recent reviews have provided valuable summaries of deep learning architectures and 
diagnostic performance benchmarks in cancer imaging, with particular emphasis on 
tumor detection, segmentation, radiomics feature extraction, and multi-modal image

analysis [ 21–24]. Many of these surveys focus on algorithmic innovation and retro -
spective performance metrics, offering detailed comparisons of model architecture and 
imaging modalities. However, diagnosis, treatment planning, and therapy monitoring 
are often discussed as largely independent components, and comparatively less attention 
is given to how ML models function across integrated, end-to-end clinical workflows. 
Furthermore, challenges related to real-world deployment such as interoperability with 
radiotherapy planning systems, regulatory approval pathways, and constraints imposed 
by real-time clinical environments are frequently acknowledged only at a high level 
rather than examined in depth.
In contrast, the present review adopts a workflow-oriented and translational perspec -
tive that maps ML methods across the full oncology imaging–treatment continuum, 
from image acquisition and tumor characterization to therapy planning, treatment 
monitoring, and adaptive intervention. Rather than organizing content solely by algo -
rithm type or imaging modality, this review emphasizes how ML models interact within 
closed-loop, feedback-driven clinical workflows that evolve over the course of treatment.
A further distinguishing feature of this review is its explicit focus on clinical trans -
lation. Key barriers to routine deployment, including workflow integration, model 
interpretability and trust, regulatory and liability considerations, and post-deployment 
monitoring, are examined in detail alongside methodological advances. Emerging par -
adigms such as explainable AI, federated learning, and quantum-enhanced machine 
learning are discussed not only as technical innovations, but also in terms of their poten-
tial to address practical deployment challenges [ 25–2

sections.title: 1.1 Literature search strategy and review methodology
sections.text:
This review was conducted as a structured narrative review with systematic elements 
to ensure comprehensive coverage of recent advances in ML–based cancer imaging and 
therapy. The literature search focused on peer-reviewed journal articles and high-impact 
conference proceedings published primarily between 2019 and 2026, with particular 
emphasis on studies from 2024 to 2026 to capture the latest developments.
Searches were performed using major scientific databases including PubMed, Web of 
Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar. Key search terms and combinations included 
machine learning, deep learning, artificial intelligence, cancer imaging, radiomics, medi-
cal image segmentation , radiotherapy planning, treatment response prediction , explain-
able AI , and federated learning . Reference lists of relevant review articles were also 
screened to identify additional pertinent studies.
Studies were selected based on their relevance to cancer imaging and therapy, meth -
odological rigor, clinical relevance, and contribution to understanding translational 
challenges. Priority was given to high-quality studies published in leading journals and 
conferences in medical imaging, oncology, and artificial intelligence. Articles focusing 
exclusively on non-oncologic imaging or lacking relevance to clinical workflows were 
excluded.
Page 4 of 31
Chow Discover Computing          (2026) 29:186 
Although this review does not follow a full PRISMA systematic review protocol or 
quantitative meta-analysis, the search and selection process was guided by PRISMA 
principles of transparency, reproducibility, and clarity [ 28]. The goal was to provide a 
balanced and critical synthesis of the literature while emphasizing emerging trends, clin-
ical translation barriers, and future research directions beyond algorithmic performance 
alone.

sections.title: 2 Fundamentals of machine learning in medical imaging
sections.text:
ML has been increasingly applied to medical imaging, offering methods to automate 
image analysis, enhance diagnostic accuracy, and optimize treatment planning. ML 
techniques are broadly categorized into supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement 
learning, each serving different purposes in image-based medical applications [ 29]. 
Moreover, DL architectures such as CNNs, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) [ 30], and 
generative adversarial networks (GANs) [ 31] have demonstrated significant potential in 
medical image processing. However, the success of these models depends on effective 
data acquisition, preprocessing, and annotation.

sections.title: 2.1 Basic concepts of machine learning in imaging
sections.text:
ML involves training algorithms to recognize patterns in medical images and make pre -
dictions based on these patterns [ 32]. In cancer imaging, ML models learn from labeled 
datasets to classify tumors, segment anatomical structures, and predict patient out -
comes. The primary ML paradigms include supervised learning, unsupervised learning, 
and reinforcement learning, each with distinct applications in medical imaging [33].
Supervised learning is widely used in medical imaging for tasks such as tumor classifi -
cation and segmentation. In this approach, models learn from labeled datasets where the 
correct output (e.g., presence or absence of a tumor) is known [ 34]. Classification mod-
els, such as support vector machines (SVMs) and DL-based CNNs, are commonly used 
for diagnosing cancer from radiological images [ 35, 36]. Segmentation models, such as 
U-Net and Mask R-CNN, help delineate tumors and other anatomical structures, assist -
ing radiologists in treatment planning [ 37, 38]. For classification tasks such as tumor 
detection, deep networks are typically optimized using cross-entropy loss [39]:

Unsupervised learning is applied when labeled data is scarce. This approach identi -

and one-class SVMs, are used for identifying rare tumor presentations or early disease 
manifestations that may not be well-represented in training datasets [42].
Reinforcement learning (RL) is gaining interest in adaptive medical imaging and treat -
ment planning. In RL, an agent learns through trial and error by interacting with an envi-
ronment and receiving feedback. Applications include optimizing imaging protocols to 
reduce radiation dose while maintaining image quality, and dynamic radiotherapy treat -
ment planning, where RL can adjust beam configurations based on tumor response over 
time [43]. Figure 1 provides a graphical comparison of the three primary ML paradigms, 
namely, supervised, unsupervised, and RL, highlighting their input requirements, learn -
ing objectives, and typical applications in cancer imaging. This visual summary comple -
ments the textual explanation by clarifying key conceptual distinctions for readers.

sections.title: 2.2 DL architectures used in medical imaging
sections.text:
DL, a subset of ML, has transformed medical imaging with its ability to learn hierarchi -
cal features directly from raw images. Several DL architectures have been applied in can-
cer imaging, each tailored to specific tasks.
CNNs are the backbone of many medical imaging applications due to their ability to 
automatically extract spatial features from images. They consist of convolutional layers 
that capture edges, textures, and complex structures, making them highly effective for 
tasks such as tumor classification and organ segmentation. CNN architectures such as 
ResNet, VGG, and DenseNet have been used in cancer detection and radiomics feature 
extraction [44].
While CNNs are effective for spatial analysis, RNNs and Transformers are useful for 
analyzing sequential medical imaging data, such as dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI and 
longitudinal scans. RNNs, particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, can

GANs have been employed in medical imaging for tasks such as image synthesis, 
denoising, and resolution enhancement. They consist of a generator network that creates 
synthetic images and a discriminator network that distinguishes real from fake images. 
GANs have been used to augment training datasets, improve image quality in low-dose 
CT scans, and generate synthetic MRI images to balance underrepresented tumor types 
in datasets [47].

sections.title: 2.3 Data acquisition and preprocessing
sections.text:
The performance of ML models in medical imaging heavily depends on data quality and 
preprocessing techniques. Proper data handling ensures that models generalize well 
across different patient populations and imaging devices.
Medical images often vary in intensity, resolution, and noise levels due to differences 
in imaging protocols and equipment. Image normalization techniques, such as his -
togram equalization and intensity standardization, help reduce variability [ 48]. Data 
augmentation methods, including rotation, flipping, and contrast adjustments, are com -
monly used to artificially increase dataset size and improve model robustness. Denoising 
techniques, such as wavelet filtering and DL-based denoising autoencoders, help remove 
artifacts and improve image clarity [49].
Medical imaging datasets are often imbalanced, with certain cancer types or tumor 
subtypes being underrepresented. Class imbalance can lead to biased ML models that 
favor the majority class. Techniques such as synthetic minority over-sampling (SMOTE) 
[50], cost-sensitive learning, and transfer learning help mitigate this issue. Moreover, 
few-shot learning approaches, including meta-learning and self-supervised learning, are 
being explored to train models with limited labeled data.
High-quality annotated datasets are essential for training reliable ML models. Image 
annotations, such as tumor boundaries or classification labels, require expert radiolo -
gists, making the annotation process time-consuming and resource-intensive. Crowd -
sourcing, semi-supervised learning, and active learning strategies are being explored to 
reduce annotation costs while maintaining accuracy [ 51]. Collaborative efforts, such as 
The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) and other publicly available medical imaging datas-
ets, play a crucial role in advancing ML research in oncology [52]. Figure 2 shows a block 
diagram summarizing the fundamentals of ML in medical imaging. The diagram catego -
rizes ML techniques with color-coded annotations to illustrate the typical application of 
each model across different cancer types.
Numerous publicly available datasets have played a critical role in advancing ML 
applications in cancer imaging. These datasets span various imaging modalities and sup -
port tasks such as tumor segmentation, lesion classification, and radiogenomics model -
ing. Table  1 summarizes representative datasets, outlining their imaging types, cancer 
focus, available annotations, and typical use cases.

Similarly, the Intersection over Union (IoU) provides a geometric measure of segmen -

tion, where spatial precision is vital [57].
In regression tasks such as predicting treatment outcomes or tumor volume changes, 
performance is typically evaluated using mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared 
error (RMSE), or R-squared values, depending on the specific application [ 58]. These 
metrics assess how closely the predicted continuous outputs align with true clinical val -
ues, such as survival duration or dose distribution.
Beyond performance metrics, validation strategies play a crucial role in assessing the 
generalizability and clinical reliability of ML models. Basic internal validation is often 
conducted using k-fold cross-validation [59], which splits the training data into multiple 
folds to assess model consistency. Holdout validation, where a separate portion of the 
dataset is reserved for final testing, is also common. However, these methods may still 
suffer from institutional bias. Therefore, external validation, using independent datasets 
from different institutions or imaging platforms, is considered essential for evaluating 
robustness across varied clinical settings.
Moreover, prospective validation through clinical trials or pilot implementations pro -
vides the most rigorous test of clinical utility [ 60]. Such evaluations help determine how 
ML models perform under real-world conditions, including integration with workflows, 
operator variability, and patient heterogeneity. Additional factors like model calibration, 
which ensures that predicted probabilities reflect true risk, and uncertainty estimation,

medical AI to support risk-aware decision-making.
Together, the use of appropriate evaluation metrics and rigorous validation strategies 
forms the foundation for developing clinically trustworthy ML systems. These practices 
not only enhance reproducibility and transparency but also build confidence among 
practitioners and regulatory bodies, facilitating the path from algorithm development to 
bedside deployment.

sections.title: 3 Machine learning applications in cancer diagnosis
sections.text:
ML has transformed cancer diagnosis by enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of image 
analysis. ML algorithms assist in detecting tumors, segmenting anatomical structures, 
extracting imaging features for predictive modeling, and integrating multi-modal imag -
ing data. Computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems further support radiologists by auto-
mating routine tasks and improving diagnostic consistency [61].

sections.title: 3.1 Tumor detection and segmentation
sections.text:
Accurate tumor detection and segmentation are critical for early diagnosis and treat -
ment planning. ML-based techniques automate these processes, improving precision 
and reducing variability across different radiologists and imaging protocols. CNNs have 
been widely used for tumor detection due to their ability to learn hierarchical image fea -
tures. Models such as ResNet, VGG, and EfficientNet have demonstrated high accuracy 
in detecting lung nodules, breast lesions, and brain tumors [ 62]. More recently, Trans-
former-based models, such as Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Swin Transformers, have 
been explored for lesion detection, leveraging self-attention mechanisms to capture 
long-range dependencies in imaging data [63].
Segmentation is crucial for outlining tumor boundaries, which impacts both diagno -
sis and treatment planning. U-Net, a widely used DL architecture, has been successfully 
applied to segment tumors in MRI, CT, and PET images. Variants such as Attention 
U-Net and nnU-Net enhance segmentation accuracy by incorporating attention mecha -
nisms, allowing the model to focus on relevant image regions [ 64, 65]. These models are 
particularly useful in radiotherapy planning, where precise delineation of tumor margins 
is required.
ML-based tumor detection and segmentation techniques have been utilized across 
various cancer types. For lung cancer, CNNs and hybrid DL models are employed to 
detect pulmonary nodules in CT scans and assess tumor progression [ 66]. In breast can-
cer, DL models aid in identifying microcalcifications and masses in mammography and 
MRI [67]. AI-based segmentation techniques are used to classify gliomas, meningiomas, 
and metastases from MRI scans in brain tumors [ 68]. For prostate cancer, ML models 
analyze multi-parametric MRI (mpMRI) to detect prostate lesions and guide biopsy 
decisions [69]. Figure 3 shows the workflow of a hybrid DL model for brain tumour clas-
sification. The model was applied to the MRI dataset for meningioma, glioma and pitu -
itary tumour [68].
DL architectures, particularly CNNs and Transformers, are preferred for tumor detec-
tion and segmentation due to their ability to automatically learn hierarchical and spatial 
features directly from raw imaging data. CNNs excel at capturing local patterns such 
as edges and textures, while Transformers leverage self-attention mechanisms to model 
Page 10 of 31
Chow Discover Computing          (2026) 29:186 
long-range dependencies, which is especially beneficial in complex anatomical contexts. 
Compared to traditional models like SVMs and random forests, DL models generally 
achieve higher accuracy in segmentation tasks and scale more efficiently with large, 
high-dimensional datasets. While SVMs and random forests require manual feature 
engineering and struggle with pixel-wise prediction, CNNs and Transformers integrate 
feature extraction and classification in an end-to-end framework, reducing preprocess -
ing overhead and improving generalization. Moreover, advances in graphics processing 
unit acceleration and parallel computing have made deep learning models more compu -
tationally efficient during inference, enabling real-time clinical applications.

sections.title: 3.2 Radiomics and feature extraction
sections.text:
Radiomics refers to the process of extracting a large number of quantitative features 
from medical images to uncover tumor characteristics that may not be visible to the 
human eye. ML models analyze these high-dimensional features to predict tumor biol -
ogy, prognosis, and response to therapy. Radiomics workflows involve extracting shape, 
texture, intensity, and wavelet-based features from medical images [ 70]. These features 
can be used for tumor classification, grading, and treatment response assessment. Fea -
ture selection techniques, such as recursive feature elimination (RFE) and principal 
component analysis (PCA), help reduce dimensionality and improve model interpret -
ability [ 71]. PCA, a dimensionality reduction technique, transforms radiomic features 
into orthogonal components that capture the most variance, making it particularly effec-
tive in modalities like MRI and PET where high-dimensional texture and intensity fea -
tures are prevalent. In contrast, RFE iteratively removes less informative features based 
on model performance, offering greater interpretability and often yielding superior

across modalities requires careful preprocessing, standardization, and alignment strate -

fusion techniques and cross-modality feature selection frameworks are being explored 
to address these challenges, enabling more robust and generalizable multi-modal 
radiomics models.
ML classifiers such as random forests, SVMs, and deep neural networks (DNNs) are 
used to distinguish between benign and malignant tumors. For example, ML models 
trained on radiomics features have been employed to predict the aggressiveness of pros -
tate cancer based on mpMRI and to classify breast lesions on mammograms [72].
Radiogenomics combines radiomic features with genomic data to uncover associations 
between imaging phenotypes and underlying molecular characteristics. As illustrated 
in Fig. 4, a representative case study demonstrates how medical imaging can be lever -
aged to predict tumor-driving gene mutations. In this study, a conditional Generative 
Adversarial Network (cGAN) was employed to generate synthetic MRI data and predict 
the mutation status of key driver genes in breast cancer patients based on radiogenomic 
analysis of MRI features [73].

sections.title: 3.3 Multi-modal imaging analysis
sections.text:
Combining data from multiple imaging modalities enhances diagnostic accuracy and 
provides a comprehensive view of tumor characteristics. DL models facilitate the fusion 
of different imaging data to improve cancer detection and staging. Different imaging 
modalities provide complementary information about tumors. For instance, PET-CT 
combines metabolic and anatomical data [ 74], while MRI and histopathology jointly 
improve tumor characterization. AI models integrate these data sources to improve 
diagnostic precision and reduce ambiguity in complex cases [ 75]. Combining PET, MRI, 
and CT data in multi-modal imaging analysis enhances cancer diagnosis by leveraging 
complementary information from each modality, structural detail from CT, soft-tissue 
contrast from MRI, and metabolic activity from PET. This integration improves lesion 
characterization, staging accuracy, and treatment planning compared to single-modality 
imaging. However, aligning and integrating heterogeneous data introduces significant 
challenges. Variations in spatial resolution, imaging protocols, and patient positioning 
can lead to misregistration and feature inconsistency. Moreover, differences in inten -
sity scales and noise profiles across modalities complicate feature fusion. Addressing 
these issues requires robust image registration algorithms, intensity normalization, and 
advanced fusion strategies such as attention-based D models. Harmonization tech -
niques and domain adaptation are also critical for mitigating variability in multi-center 
datasets, ensuring that integrated models generalize effectively across diverse clinical 
environments.
Fusion models use DL to merge features from different modalities. For example, CNN-
based feature fusion models combine PET and MRI data for improved glioblastoma seg -
mentation, while Transformer-based multi-modal networks integrate histopathological 
and radiological images for breast cancer diagnosis [76].
Page 12 of 31
Chow Discover Computing          (2026) 29:186 
Multi-modal ML models are used to assess metastatic disease and treatment efficacy. 
AI algorithms analyzing whole-body PET-CT scans detect distant metastases in lung 
and prostate cancer, while DL models track tumor changes over time in longitudinal 
imaging studies [77].

sections.title: 3.4 CAD systems
sections.text:
CAD systems use ML to assist radiologists in diagnosing cancer, reducing interpretation 
variability and improving workflow efficiency. These systems are particularly valuable 
in screening programs, where large volumes of imaging data must be analyzed. ML-
powered CAD systems highlight suspicious lesions, rank possible diagnoses, and pro -
vide confidence scores to support clinical decision-making [ 78]. These systems are used 
in both 2D and 3D imaging, helping radiologists prioritize high-risk cases for further 
review [79].

AI-assisted mammography and lung nodule detection have shown significant advance-
ments. For mammography, AI algorithms developed by organizations like Google Health 
[80] and DeepMind [ 81] assist in detecting breast cancer by analyzing mammograms 
with accuracy comparable to expert radiologists. In lung nodule detection, CAD systems 
for chest CT scans, such as those used in the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST), 
enhance the detection of early-stage lung cancer by flagging suspicious nodules [82].
Studies have shown that AI-assisted diagnosis improves sensitivity and specific -
ity while reducing false positives and false negatives [ 83–85]. ML models help mitigate 
inter-observer variability and enhance efficiency, particularly in high-volume screening 
settings. However, challenges remain in ensuring interpretability and gaining regulatory 
approval for widespread clinical adoption.
Comparative evaluations indicate that AI-assisted imaging can complement expert 
readers, reduce inter-observer variability, and lower error rates in routine practice. In 
population breast screening, a nationwide deployment reported that radiologists using 
AI triage detected more cancers with fewer false-positive recalls than standard double 
reading, suggesting improved specificity without loss of sensitivity [ 86]. Similarly, in 
chest radiography, an AI “second reader” identified false-negative examinations initially 
reported as normal, demonstrating potential to reduce misses in day-to-day workflow 
[87]. Beyond single-task readers, multi-annotator/ensemble frameworks have shown 
higher segmentation accuracy than any single annotator, offering a practical path to 
standardize labels and mitigate inter-reader variation [ 88]. Professional guidance from 
major radiology societies further recommends continuous registry-based monitoring 
of sensitivity/specificity and subgroup performance after deployment, to limit drift and 
sustain clinical safety, reinforcing that AI is most effective as a calibrated, audited aid to 
expert judgment rather than a replacement [89].

sections.title: 4 Machine learning in cancer therapy planning and monitoring
sections.text:
ML is transforming cancer therapy by improving treatment planning, monitoring 
therapeutic response, and guiding real-time interventions. AI-driven models enhance 
radiotherapy planning, predict treatment outcomes, and optimize image-guided inter -
ventions, leading to more personalized and adaptive cancer treatments.

sections.title: 4.1 AI-assisted radiotherapy planning
sections.text:
Radiotherapy is a cornerstone of cancer treatment, requiring precise dose delivery to 
tumor tissues while sparing healthy organs. ML algorithms automate and optimize RT 
planning by segmenting anatomical structures, predicting optimal dose distributions, 
and enabling adaptive treatment strategies. Accurate segmentation of tumor volumes 
and OARs is crucial for radiotherapy planning. DL models, particularly CNN-based 
architectures such as U-Net and DeepLab, have been widely used for automatic con -
touring in MRI and CT scans [ 90]. These models reduce variability in manual delinea -
tion and enhance treatment consistency. Transformer-based segmentation models are 
also emerging, offering improved long-range spatial dependencies for precise boundary 
detection [91].
AI models facilitate automated dose distribution prediction and treatment plan 
optimization. Neural networks and reinforcement learning approaches analyze his -
torical treatment plans to generate dose-volume histograms (DVHs) and optimize

intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) and volumetric modulated arc therapy 
(VMAT) plans [ 92, 93]. These models improve dose conformity and reduce planning 
time while maintaining high treatment quality. Adaptive radiotherapy (ART) can signifi-
cantly benefit from real-time AI-driven adjustments based on continuous imaging feed -
back. By integrating AI models into ART workflows, treatment plans can be dynamically 
updated in response to anatomical or physiological changes observed during therapy, 
such as tumor shrinkage or organ motion. For example, daily MRI or CBCT scans can 
feed into deep learning models that predict dose distribution and automatically re-opti -
mize beam configurations, reducing the need for manual replanning [ 94]. This closed-
loop system enhances treatment precision, minimizes toxicity to surrounding organs, 
and supports personalized therapy by adapting to patient-specific changes over the 
course of treatment. Clinically, such an approach could improve local control rates and 
reduce adverse effects, but it requires robust automation, real-time computation, and 
rigorous validation to ensure safety and regulatory compliance.

sections.title: 4.2 Predicting treatment response from imaging
sections.text:
Predicting treatment response is essential for guiding therapeutic decisions and per -
sonalizing cancer care. ML models extract imaging-based biomarkers to assess tumor 
response, anticipate treatment-related toxicities, and refine patient-specific therapeutic 
strategies [ 95]. Radiomics and DL models analyze pre- and post-treatment imaging to 
identify predictive biomarkers of therapy response. For example, texture features from 
MRI and PET scans are correlated with tumor radiosensitivity, while AI-driven feature 
selection enhances predictive accuracy [96].
AI is playing a growing role in immunotherapy response assessment. ML mod -
els analyze radiomics features and genetic data to predict patient response to immune 
checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) [ 97]. DL also assists in personalizing targeted therapies by 
integrating imaging, genomics, and clinical data to identify optimal treatment strategies 
[98].
ML models predict radiation-induced toxicities such as pneumonitis, mucositis, and 
fibrosis. AI-driven dose-response modeling helps identify patients at risk of severe side 
effects, enabling proactive treatment modifications to minimize toxicity while maintain -
ing therapeutic efficacy [99].
Effective treatment monitoring is not only about assessing response but also about 
informing timely and adaptive intervention. In clinical practice, imaging-based response 
assessments, such as MRI performed every 48–72  h, provide critical insights that can 
trigger changes in therapeutic strategy, such as treatment intensification or replanning 
of radiotherapy. However, the true clinical value lies in closing the loop: using monitor -
ing data to guide interventions and then recalibrating AI models based on post-inter -
vention imaging. This iterative feedback mechanism allows AI systems to dynamically 
update confidence scores and predictive outputs based on new anatomical or physiologi-
cal changes.
RL provides a powerful framework for implementing AI-driven adaptive radiotherapy 
systems that continuously refine treatment strategies based on imaging feedback and 
observed outcomes. In this approach, the AI agent interacts with the treatment envi -
ronment, where each adjustment, such as modifying dose distribution or beam angles, 
is evaluated through a reward function linked to tumor control and toxicity reduction.
